summary.text: Rome ruled lands around the Mediterranean and across much of Europe, Western Asia and North Africa in classical times.
It began when Octavian beat Mark Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BC, then received the title Augustus in 27 BC as the first emperor.
The Western half collapsed in 476 AD, while the Eastern half, called the Byzantine Empire, lasted until Constantinople fell in 1453.

facts.label: First emperor
facts.value: Octavian became Augustus, the first Roman emperor, in 27 BC

facts.label: Greatest extent
facts.value: Reached its largest size under Trajan, who ruled 98 to 117 AD

facts.label: Western collapse
facts.value: 476 AD, when Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustus

facts.label: Eastern survival
facts.value: The Byzantine Empire lasted until Constantinople fell in 1453

facts.label: Third-century crisis
facts.value: Fifty years of civil war, plagues and invasions

items.prompt: A province in the Roman world belongs to the emperor himself. Who would be running it day to day?
items.explain: Imperial provinces belonged to the emperor and were governed by legates, while senatorial provinces had proconsuls appointed by lot each year.

items.prompt: A Roman general is given an honorary title meaning 'commander'. Which later word of rank comes from that custom?
items.explain: The title imperator was given to successful consuls or generals, and it was always bestowed on the early emperors, which is where the word emperor comes from.

items.prompt: In the years just after 27 BC, Rome still has its Senate and its elected magistrates. Who actually holds all meaningful authority?

options.label: The consuls, who are elected each year
The Senate, which meets as it always did
The man the Senate has just named Augustus

items.explain: The republic stood in name, but Augustus had all meaningful authority after the Senate gave him his new title.

items.prompt: In 476 a Germanic king removes the last emperor in Italy. Where does Roman rule carry on, for roughly another thousand years?

options.label: At Constantinople, in the Eastern Empire
At Palmyra, under its own rulers

items.explain: The Eastern Roman Empire survived with Constantinople as its sole capital until 1453; Ravenna had fallen to the Herulians.

items.prompt: The civil wars of the 3rd century ended with Diocletian's victory. How did he arrange imperial government afterward?

options.label: A single court moved to Byzantium
Two courts, one Greek East and one Latin West
A restored Republic led by the Senate

items.explain: Diocletian set up two different imperial courts in the Greek East and the Latin West; moving the seat to Byzantium came later under Constantine.

items.prompt: Rome's government left a mark on the early United States. Which part of it?

options.label: Rule by emperors from Augustus on

items.explain: Rome's republican institutions influenced medieval Italian city-state republics, the early United States and modern democratic republics.

pack.title: From Republic to Emperor
pack.question: How did a republic run by elected officials become an empire ruled by one person?

beats.title: From Republic to Emperor
beats.hook: Rome kept its Senate and its offices, yet one man held all the real power.

beats.prompt: Put these events from Rome's turn from republic to empire in order

items.label: Julius Caesar is briefly perpetual dictator (44 BC)
Antony and Octavian defeat Caesar's killers at Philippi (42 BC)
Octavian defeats Antony and Cleopatra at Actium (31 BC)
The Senate gives Octavian the title Augustus (27 BC)

beats.explain: Caesar's rule and killing came first, then the victory at Philippi, then Actium, and finally the Senate's grant of the title Augustus.

beats.prompt: In 27 BC the Senate gives one man a new title and the right to command. Elections and the Senate carry on as before. Where does meaningful authority sit?
beats.explain: Although the republic stood in name, Augustus had all meaningful authority.

choices.label: With the new titleholder, even though the republic stands in name
With the Senate, because it granted the title
choices.feedback: Granting the title looks like power, but the titleholder ended up with all meaningful authority.

choices.label: With the consuls, because they are still elected each year
choices.feedback: The offices still exist, which makes this tempting, but they no longer hold the real power.

beats.prompt: Match each Roman term to its meaning

right.label: Honorary title for a commander, the origin of 'emperor'
Governed by a proconsul appointed by lot each year
The Roman legal idea of command, typically military
Belonged to the emperor and was governed by a legate

beats.explain: Each term names a piece of how Rome was commanded and governed.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?

steps.text: The Western Roman Empire collapsed in 476 AD.
The Eastern Roman Empire, also called the Byzantine Empire, had Constantinople as its capital.
Because the West fell, the East must have fallen in the same year.
So Roman rule ended everywhere in 476.

beats.explain: The Eastern Empire did not fall with the West; it survived until Constantinople fell in 1453.

paragraphs.heading: What the empire was
paragraphs.text: The Roman Empire was a state whose power dominated the Mediterranean in the classical period, along with much of Europe, North Africa and Western Asia. Most of these lands had already been conquered by the Roman Republic, the Roman state that came before it. Rule by one person became permanent after Octavian rose to power. In 27 BC the Senate gave him overarching military power, called imperium, and the new title Augustus, making him the first Roman emperor.

paragraphs.heading: From republic to emperor
paragraphs.text: By 100 BC Rome ruled from the Italian peninsula across most of the Mediterranean and beyond. The Republic was not a nation in today's sense but a network of self-governing towns and of provinces run by army commanders, led by yearly elected officials, above all the consuls, together with the Senate. Civil wars and political quarrels shook it badly. In 44 BC Julius Caesar was briefly dictator for life before a group opposed to his power killed him. Octavian, Caesar's adopted son, later beat the forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BC.

paragraphs.heading: An emperor in old clothes
paragraphs.text: The Senate made Augustus princeps, meaning "foremost", and the republic went on in name while he held all real power. The word emperor comes from imperator, "commander", an honorary title given to successful generals and always given to the early emperors. Rome's vast lands were split into senatorial provinces, run by proconsuls chosen by lot each year, and imperial provinces, which belonged to the emperor and were run by legates. Over his 40 years in charge a new order took shape, so that Tiberius could follow him as monarch in all but name.

paragraphs.heading: Peace, then trouble
paragraphs.text: The first two centuries brought a stability and wealth Rome had never had before, known as the Pax Romana, or "Roman Peace". Revolts in the provinces were rare and were crushed quickly. Rome reached its largest size under Trajan, who ruled from 98 to 117 AD. Trouble and decline set in under Commodus, who ruled from 180 to 192.

paragraphs.heading: Crisis and division
paragraphs.text: In the 3rd century a 50-year crisis of civil war, plague and barbarian invasion threatened the empire's survival. The Gallic and Palmyrene empires broke away and short-lived emperors came and went, until Aurelian reunited the whole. Diocletian ended the civil wars and set up two imperial courts, one in the Greek East and one in the Latin West. Constantine the Great, the first Christian emperor, shifted the imperial seat in 330 from Rome to Byzantium and renamed it Constantinople.

paragraphs.heading: The West falls, the East lasts
paragraphs.text: During the Migration Period, large invasions by Germanic peoples and the Huns brought the western empire into decline. In 476 Ravenna fell to the Germanic Herulians and Odoacer removed the emperor Romulus Augustus, and the Western Empire collapsed. The Eastern Roman Empire, also called the Byzantine Empire, survived for another thousand years with Constantinople as its only capital. It ended when that city fell in 1453.

paragraphs.heading: What Rome left behind
paragraphs.text: Because the empire was so large and lasted so long, its institutions and culture shaped law, religion, language, art, philosophy, literature, architecture and government across its lands. Classical science and technology, the basis on which Islamic science was built, were rediscovered in medieval Europe and helped bring about the Scientific Renaissance and the Scientific Revolution. Rome's republican institutions influenced the city-state republics of medieval Italy, the early United States and modern democratic republics.
